explanation: Fires most on ' St' as the start of a proper-name place or institution (St Paul's School, St. Stanislaus, Church of St Mary, St. Louis), and also on the first subword pieces of other multi-token names or words (Cerro Az|ul, Obreros y Campesinos, isonia|z|id, molybdenum dis|ulfide, cry|ost|atic, and Finnish, Romanian or Greek word fragments). Other tokens fire weakly at most.

Fires on an auxiliary or modal verb (am, is, are, have, will, can, was, has) when it begins a question with subject-auxiliary inversion, strongest after 'what', 'or', 'but' or 'and' in a question ('what am I doing wrong', 'or is it', 'and have we lost'). Inverted 'do/does' or a sentence-initial 'Is/Do' fires moderately; ordinary declarative auxiliaries fire weakly.

Fires at boundary positions that end a title, heading, dateline or short header and lead into body text: the '\n\n' after a title line, ')' closing a dateline like 'DETROIT (WXYZ)', the last digit of a year in a title, and the last word of a title phrase. Fires moderately on punctuation that ends a question or clause before new text starts.

Diffuse. Fires on tokens in the middle of technical or code identifiers and compound terms (layout_constraint, dependency injection, android.content.Context, NSSQLite, nanograms, focus group, Manifest Destiny) and on scattered function words in prose. I found no clear single trigger.

Mostly fires on police and arrest-news wording: 'arrested', 'Arrested', 'taken into custody', 'pulled him over', 'caught', 'drove away from' an accident scene, and on tokens in crime-report sentences. Also fires on assorted unrelated compound pieces (Tokyo College of Music, hive, borderline personality, prehospital, domesticated).

Fires on quantifier or determiner words, mainly 'all' (also 'any', 'such', 'each', 'a' in 'a number of' or 'ranging from a'), especially floating 'all' after a plural subject ('were all lower', 'have all made') or 'all' at the start of a word ('alligator', 'allodynia'). The top example is a Cyrillic word fragment, which looks like an outlier.

Fires on the second item of a coordinated or contrastive pair, i.e. the token right after 'and', 'or', 'rather than', or a comma in parallel structures (dest1, ... dest2; 'atopic dermatitis and psoriasis'; acronym starts like '(PD', '(FG'). Also fires on many other mid-sentence content tokens in technical text. Broad and noisy.

Fires on statement-starting keywords and line-break boundaries in code, especially procedural or SQL/Pascal/Basic-style code: 'to' in 'for i=2 to n', the newline after 'then' or 'else', 'end;', 'RETURN', 'DECLARE', 'PUBLIC', 'if', and closing ')' of a function signature. Prose fires weakly.

Fires on short subword fragments inside long, rare or foreign words split into several tokens, especially medical or Latin-Greek terms ('oc' in lymphocytosis, varicocoele, Streptococcus, Monocerotis; 'ic' in pericardium) and Scandinavian, German or Esperanto word pieces. Whole common words do not fire.

Mixed. Fires on 'workers' after a number or descriptor ('400 IT workers', '700 workers'), on the final subword piece of person surnames or names (Fol|es, Cant|or, Proff|itt, C|ech, Russ|el), on trailing zeros of large money figures, and on assorted words in informal prose ('like any other', 'he's').

Fires on sentence-ending punctuation (mostly '.', also '?' or '!') that closes a short, punchy, informal or opinionated sentence in conversational prose (comments, blogs, forum posts), right before a new sentence starts. A period at the end of formal or scientific sentences fires only weakly or moderately.

Diffuse. Fires on tokens that continue fixed phrases or multi-token words ('move on', 'piece of', 'so far so', 'jsfiddle', 'dissonance', 'Minimally', 'unsophisticated', 'black mold') and on various code tokens (whitespace runs, 'error', 'where'). I found no consistent single trigger.

Fires on the subject or first token of a new clause, often a pronoun (I, you, we, our, it, there) right after a conjunction ('but', 'or', 'if', 'wherever') or a clause-separating comma or semicolon, i.e. where a new clause's subject is about to come. Content tokens in noun phrases fire weakly.

Mixed. Fires on boilerplate and citation-like contexts (license headers: 'LICENSE file', 'file that was distributed', 'Use of', 'distribution'; stack traces: 'in'; 'et al'; 'MEMORANDUM AND ORDER'; dotted version numbers) and on assorted words in prose ('high diversity', '12 million'). No single clear concept.

Fires on index or subscript variables in math and code, i.e. the token inside brackets or subscripts like a[i], X_{n}, x^{n-1}, aXi-1, C_{N,r}. Weaker side activity on 'redistributed' or 'published' in copyright boilerplate and on 'Share this post/article'.

Fires on philosophy and academic-theory contexts, strongest on 'philosopher' and on 'ph'/'Ph' pieces (phobia, philo, Ph.D., epiphany, PHIL), with moderate firing on prepositions in theoretical or physics discussion ('description by', 'units of information in'). Part of it looks driven by the letters 'ph' rather than the topic.

Diffuse. Fires on later pieces of multi-token terms (atax|ia, Gal|era, pain|less, Pri|us, amy|ot|rophic), on 'me' after verbs ('let me', 'struck me', 'believe me'), and on game-score digits ('2-0', '7-3', '27-12'). These look like unrelated triggers.

Fires strongly on ')' closing a wire-service dateline ('BEIJING (AP)', 'LONDON (Reuters)') and, more broadly, on the token where the main clause continues after an opening frame in news-like or expository text ('a feature that will', 'Collect the terms in', 'wanted to', 'Glad to'). The dateline part is crisp; the rest is diffuse.

Fires on tokens inside code loop headers and array declarations: the loop variable 'i' after 'for(i=0;', '<' in 'i < n', 'range' in 'for i in range', '[' in char arrays like 'vendor[16]', 'new char[9]', plus separators in index ranges like '1:8' or '1..3'. Code outside loops or indexing fires weakly.

Fires on labels or keys in structured and list-like text, i.e. field names and headings that come before a value or new section ('Images:', 'Mobile', 'Telephone', 'Shipping Information', 'Screenshots', 'Restrictions:', '@version', JSON keys like 'stringArray'). It also fires on assorted name endings (Barrowman, Shandong). Noisy.

Fires on punctuation and structural tokens inside or right next to CJK (Chinese or Japanese) text: full-width colons, brackets 「, commas ，, 年, an opening '(' before Chinese characters, '">' before a Chinese string value, '/**' before a Chinese comment. ASCII-only contexts fire weakly.
